note: The strange tree of Canto 22, hung with fruit and wet with spray, from which a hidden voice called out examples of temperance. Dante is peering in to find the speaker.
Hunting songbirds with nets or snares, a common pastime, and for Dante a picture of time thrown away.

context: Dante's names for Virgil grow more tender as the time of their parting comes near. It is four cantos away.

note: Virgil and Statius, the Roman poet who joined them in Canto 21. They are still talking of poetry.

From Psalm 51, the great psalm of repentance: "O Lord, open thou my lips, and my mouth shall show forth thy praise." The prayer fits the sin. Mouths once used for eating and drinking too much are now opened to praise God.
The penance each soul owes for its sins. Paying it is pictured as untying a knot.
The souls of Purgatory are pilgrims on the way to their true home. These do not stop, because their penance is to keep walking round the terrace.

quote: skin took its shape from bone
note: The contrapasso of the gluttons. They fed the body beyond need, and now they starve until nothing but skin covers the bone.

A prince of Thessaly in Ovid's Metamorphoses. He cut down an oak sacred to the goddess Ceres, and she sent Famine to fill him with a hunger nothing could satisfy. He ate up all he owned, sold his own daughter for food, and at last began to eat his own body.
The Jews besieged in Jerusalem by the Roman army under Titus in AD 70. The city was starved before it fell.

quote: Mary made prey of her own son
note: Not the Virgin. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of a woman named Mary who, mad with hunger during the siege, killed her baby son and ate him. Dante's word for what she did is that of a bird of prey: she "set her beak" in him.

Omo is "man" in Dante's Italian, from the Latin homo. A medieval notion held that God wrote the word on every human face: the eyes are the two O's, and the line of the brows and nose, with the cheekbones, makes a rounded M between them. On these starved faces the M stands out.

The Italian is most often read as: who would believe it, not knowing how it comes about? The puzzle is Dante's own. These are shades, with no bodies to feed. How can they starve? He puts the question in Canto 25.

quote: What grace is this for me?
note: The shade is overjoyed to see a living friend here, in the flesh.

context: Hunger has changed his face so much that Dante knows him only by his voice. In their youth the two traded sonnets in which Dante mocked his friend's greed at table.

note: Not the disease. His skin is dry, scaly and discolored from starvation.

quote: which I wept over when you died
note: Forese died in 1296, and Dante was evidently at his deathbed or his funeral. Whatever insults they once traded, the friendship was real.
The will of God, which gives the tree and the water their power to waken hunger and thirst.
Made holy again. The suffering here does not punish for its own sake. It cures the habit of the sin.
There is more than one such tree on the terrace. The travelers come to another in Canto 24. Each time the souls pass one, their hunger is sharpened again.
The souls of Purgatory want their pain, because it is making them fit for Heaven. Forese corrects himself in the middle of his sentence.

Christ's cry on the cross: "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani", "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). He went willingly to his death to save mankind. The souls go to the tree as he went to the cross, which was often called a tree, suffering gladly.
Forese died in July 1296. The journey takes place in the spring of 1300.
Repentance. Dante knows that Forese went on sinning until he was too ill to sin any more, and turned to God only at the very end.

quote: where time makes restitution for time
note: Ante-Purgatory, the lower slopes of the mountain. Those who put off repentance until their last hour must wait there as long as they lived before they may begin their penance (Canto 4). Forese should still be waiting.

Forese's wife. Prayers of the living shorten a soul's time in Purgatory, a rule stated in Cantos 3 and 6. In one of his mocking sonnets to Forese, Dante had made fun of her as a neglected wife, coughing with cold in an empty bed. This warm praise is usually read as his apology.
Wormwood is a very bitter herb. The pain is bitter, and sweet because of what it leads to.
Ante-Purgatory again. Her prayers spared him the wait, and the lower terraces as well.
A tender diminutive in the Italian, vedovella.
A wild mountain district in the middle of Sardinia. Its people had a name for savagery, and its women were said to go about half naked.

quote: the Barbagia I left her in
note: Florence. Forese says the women of his own city are more shameless than those of the Sardinian mountains.

Forese foresees preachers forbidding Florentine women their low-cut dresses. Laws and church rulings against immodest dress were common in Italian cities of the time, and scholars are not sure which one Dante has in mind.

context: Almost every Florentine whom Dante meets in the afterlife has something hard to say about the city. Forese's complaint is about its women.

note: The medieval Christian name for Muslims, especially Arabs. The point of the taunt is that even peoples the Florentines looked down on dress decently without being ordered to.

quote: what swift Heaven prepares for them
note: A prophecy of disaster for Florence. Like all the prophecies in the poem, it was written after the event. The city suffered many blows in the years after 1300. This one is often linked to the bloody defeat of the Florentines at Montecatini in 1315.
Before a child who is a baby in 1300 is old enough to grow a beard: within about fifteen years.
Dante casts a shadow. The dead do not, and all through Purgatory the souls are amazed to see that he is alive.

quote: what you were with me and I with you
note: A confession. Dante looks back with shame on the life the two led together when they were young. The coarse sonnets they exchanged are usually taken as a sign of it. Many readers connect this period with the "dark forest" of Inferno 1.
Dante says only "the other day". Virgil came to him in the dark forest five days before this. It is now the Tuesday after Easter.

quote: the sister of the one over there
note: The moon. In classical myth the moon goddess Diana is the sister of Apollo, god of the sun. The moon was full on the night Dante was lost in the forest (Inferno 20).
The damned in Hell, who are dead in soul as well as body. The souls of Purgatory are on their way to eternal life.
Sin bends the soul out of shape, and the mountain makes it straight again.

context: Dante names her to Forese with no explanation: an old friend from Florence would know who she was. She will meet him at the top of the mountain (Canto 30), and Virgil will go no further.
Dante does not give his name. The mountain shook when his penance ended (Cantos 20–21).
